problem: RL-based mapless navigation from camera-only input suffers from sparse rewards, unstable training and poor performance in partially observable, cluttered scenes; prior RL+scene-graph works do not combine graphs with imitation and curriculum learning for continuous velocity control.
motivation: A 3D scene graph gives object-level spatial priors that help predict the target location under partial observability. Imitation learning (expert demos) avoids local minima and curriculum learning stabilizes training, so combining all three should improve success in hard cases.
key_idea: Feed a CLIP-similarity-weighted pooled open-vocabulary 3D scene graph (ConceptGraph/BBQ) into a SAC policy trained with a difficulty curriculum and 30% expert (Dijkstra + Pure Pursuit) episodes.
insight: The scene graph gain is small on easy settings but grows to about 10-20 points at larger initial distances (Table 1: complex stage 84% vs 67% at 2 m). Weighting all scene objects by CLIP similarity to the target (SGN-CIRL scene, 89.8% avg) beats using only the target node (85.4%) and no graph (82.4%). With randomly placed chairs, plain RL with the graph reaches only 21% versus 82% with SGN-CIRL, though that uses manually built ground-truth graphs and the two rows differ in IL/CL, so the graph's effect is confounded.
method: 3D scene graph construction: RGB-D 1280x720 sequences from Isaac Sim are processed by ConceptGraph (YOLO) or BBQ to get per-object text descriptions and 3D boxes (extent+position).

Graph encoder: each object is a 518-d vector (512-d CLIP text embedding + 6-d box); cosine similarity to the CLIP embedding of the target is used as weights to pool the (num_objects,518) graph into one vector.
SAC policy: continuous linear/angular velocity output; observation is current velocity plus CLIP embeddings of the camera image, text command and scene graph; trained with stable-baselines3.

Curriculum learning: difficulty is (initial distance R in [0,3] m, angle error phi); if success over last 30 non-IL episodes exceeds 85%, phi is increased, otherwise phi is reset to 0 and R is increased.
Imitation learning control module: Dijkstra paths on a grid of admissible positions to candidate target positions, simplified, followed by Pure Pursuit; used in 30% of training episodes.
Reward: sparse (-0.2 no subtask, -0.1 one subtask, +2 second subtask, -5 on timeout/collision); success means angle error <=13 degrees and distance error <=1.1 m.

setting.backbone: SAC policy trained from scratch on frozen CLIP embeddings; scene graph from ConceptGraph (YOLO) / BBQ
setting.training_data: RL in Isaac Sim, 650k timesteps (simple scene, no control module), 500k timesteps (complex scene); 30% expert Dijkstra+Pure Pursuit episodes; no external data
setting.observation: monocular RGB 400x400 from two cameras + CLIP text goal + current velocity + 3D scene graph
setting.privileged: scene graph built beforehand from scene data; manually created ground-truth graphs in the random-obstacle experiment; expert demos use map/positions in training only

numbers.method: RL with scene graph (no control module)
numbers.extra: curriculum learning, no imitation module; 650k timesteps; init. distance error 2 m / 2.4 m

numbers_note: Custom, non-standard Isaac Sim scenes; results are also given in figures; no public benchmark numbers. Baseline no-graph averages are 71.5% (simple) and 82.4% (complex).
results: In the complex scene, SGN-CIRL (scene) reaches 89.8% average SR vs 82.4% for RL without graph, and 84% vs 67% at 2 m initial distance. In the simple scene, the graph gives 78.6% vs 71.5%. With random chairs and ground-truth graphs, SR is 82% vs 21% for RL with scene graph.
limitations: Only small custom Isaac Sim scenes with a single target (bowl); no standard benchmarks, no real robot, no comparison with other published methods.
Ablations are confounded and incomplete (the 21% vs 82% comparison also differs in IL/CL and uses manual ground-truth graphs; no IL-only or CL-only ablation; no variance/seeds reported).
Scene graph is static and prebuilt; dynamic scenes are left to future work.
